name: biski64
workload: Raw PRNG next()-call throughput (bytes/sec) for 64-bit generators, measured with Google Benchmark across 8 threads in the planet36/prng-test-bench harness.
claimed_speedup: ~2.5x biski64 vs std::mt19937_64 (13.9-14.0 GB/s vs 5.5-5.6 GB/s), ~2.8x vs std::mt19937 (~5.0 GB/s) (derived from page data: results/prng-next-benchmark.json, 'threads:7' entries)
compiler_and_flags: g++, -std=c++26 -O3 -flto=auto -march=native (per repo Makefile); Google Benchmark v1.9.5 release build
hardware: 8-vCPU Linux VM (hostname 'arch-vm'), 2419 MHz; exact CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 152 stars; published as the biski64 crate on crates.io
tradeoffs: Newer, less battle-tested design than PCG/xoshiro; not cryptographically secure; guarantees only a 2^64 minimum period (smaller than xoshiro256's 2^256); author's own README benchmarks it against xoshiro/xoroshiro/PCG/wyrand/Java generators, not directly against std::mt19937.
caveats: The std::mt19937 comparison comes from an independent third-party benchmark (planet36/prng-test-bench), not biski64's own README, whose own numbers (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D, vs xoshiro/PCG/wyrand/sfc64/Java) don't include std::mt19937 directly. The third-party benchmark's hardware is a generic 8-vCPU VM with no stated CPU model, which caps the tier below A despite public code and stated compiler/flags.
found_via: gh search repos 'fast random number generator C++' -> planet36/prng-test-bench (active PRNG shootout, harvested biski64 as a winner) -> gh search repos 'biski64' -> danielcota/biski64

name: AESRand
workload: 5-10 billion-iteration tight loop generating random bytes summed into an anti-optimizer accumulator, timed with QueryPerformanceCounter, CPU clock locked to remove turbo-boost noise.
claimed_speedup: 27.45 GB/s (single-stream) / 34.35 GB/s (dual-stream) for AESRand vs 0.858 GB/s for std::mt19937 (~32x / ~40x throughput; derived from page data in BenchmarkResults.md); on a cycles-per-iteration basis, 3.69 cycles/iter (32 bytes/iter) vs mt19937's 14.76 cycles/iter (4 bytes/iter), ~4x fewer cycles per call (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (Windows build); no explicit optimization flags stated beyond 'built in VS2017'
hardware: AMD Threadripper 1950x, manually locked to 3.4 GHz (verified in Ryzen Master)
tradeoffs: Requires AES-NI hardware (x86 since Westmere/Bulldozer; author notes Power9/ARM would need adaptation); prototype/research quality rather than a packaged library; author flags a 1-bit-change statistical weakness and that the parallel-stream variant fails PractRand beyond 8TB.
caveats: Author's own benchmark notes explicitly that std::mt19937 'was NOT inlined' by MSVC in the test, which may inflate mt19937's measured cost and the resulting speedup ratio; first-party, single-machine result with no independent replication; exact compiler optimization flags not given.
found_via: gh search code 'faster than std::mt19937' -> dragontamer/AESRand README.md: 'Faster than xoshiro256plus, pcg32, and std::mt19937'

name: nanobench::Rng (RomuDuoJr)
workload: Generating 64-bit random values via Rng::operator(); author's own in-header micro-benchmark comparing nanobench's built-in RomuDuoJr-based Rng against std::default_random_engine and std::mt19937_64.
claimed_speedup: "In my benchmark, this is ~46 times faster than std::default_random_engine ... the fastest std contender is std::mt19937_64. Still, this RNG is 2-3 times as fast." (verbatim from header doc comment)
stars_or_usage: 1,738 stars; widely used C++ micro-benchmarking library
tradeoffs: Rng is not cryptographically secure and has a modest estimated capacity (~2^51 bytes); designed for benchmarking workloads rather than general-purpose simulation where xoshiro/PCG-class statistical guarantees may be wanted; author notes the underlying algorithm may change between nanobench releases.
caveats: The speedup figure is a first-party claim inside a Doxygen doc comment ('In my benchmark...'); no benchmark code, numbers table, hardware, or compiler is published alongside it in the repo, so it cannot be independently reproduced.
found_via: gh search code 'faster than std::mt19937' surfaced a vendored copy of this comment in ktprime/emhash:bench/nanobench.h; traced to and confirmed against the canonical martinus/nanobench source (src/include/nanobench.h, Rng::operator() doc comment)

name: nanobench::Rng::shuffle()
workload: Shuffling a container's elements using nanobench's Rng::bounded() draw (Lemire fast-range technique) inside the Fisher-Yates loop instead of std::uniform_int_distribution.
claimed_speedup: "preferable to std::shuffle because it is over 5 times faster" (verbatim from header doc comment)
tradeoffs: Uses a biased bounded-random draw instead of std::uniform_int_distribution, so the shuffle is not perfectly uniform (bias described as negligible except for ranges close to UINT32_MAX); shares the underlying RomuDuoJr generator's non-cryptographic quality.
caveats: First-party claim in a doc comment with no accompanying benchmark code, numbers, hardware, or compiler info in the repo; the '5 times faster' figure is unverified from the source itself.
found_via: Same nanobench.h source as the Rng entry, adjacent doc comment for the shuffle() member function (src/include/nanobench.h, Rng::shuffle doc comment)
